method: Each channel is modelled as a block of spectrum centred on the channel number: 20 MHz wide in 5 and 6 GHz and 22 MHz wide in 2.4 GHz, the width the original 802.11 mask occupies on that 5 MHz channel grid, with centres at 2412 MHz plus 5 MHz per 2.4 GHz channel, 5000 MHz plus 5 MHz per 5 GHz channel and 5950 MHz plus 5 MHz per 6 GHz channel. A 40, 80 or 160 MHz channel is formed from two, four or eight contiguous 20 MHz channels and centred on their mean, so its centre is a half or whole channel number and its block spans the members. Contiguity is checked in spectrum, not in list order: the 20 MHz gap between channels 144 and 149 ends a run, so a 160 MHz channel can only be 50 or 114 in the 5 GHz band. A neighbouring network is entered as its primary channel, optionally with :40, :80 or :160, and is resolved to the block that contains that primary; widths above the planned width are allowed, so a wide neighbour can cover a narrow channel completely. The overlap is the shared width of the two blocks in MHz, congestion is that overlap as a percentage of the planned block capped at 100, co-channel networks are those whose block is identical, and overlapping networks are those sharing any spectrum. Channels are ranked by overlap, then fewest co-channel networks, then channel number. The plan takes the quietest channel and then the quietest channel sharing no spectrum with those already chosen, up to four access points, and reports when the band cannot hold that many, which is why at most three 2.4 GHz radios fit side by side. Limits: 2.4 GHz is modelled at 20 MHz only, 5 and 6 GHz at 20, 40, 80 and 160 MHz; up to 24 neighbours; 1 to 4 access points. Signal strength, walls, distance, antenna patterns, DFS radar rules, regional channel availability and client capabilities are not modelled, so a channel that looks clear here still needs a check against local radio regulations. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: IEEE 802.11 channelisation: 2.4 GHz channels sit on a 5 MHz grid and occupy a 22 MHz mask, so only channels five apart (1, 6 and 11) leave no shared spectrum.
5 GHz 20 MHz channels sit 20 MHz apart, and 40, 80 and 160 MHz channels are formed from contiguous 20 MHz channels; the 20 MHz gap between channels 144 and 149 splits the usable runs.
6 GHz 20 MHz channels are numbered 1 to 233 in steps of 4 at 20 MHz spacing, giving 29 channels of 40 MHz, 14 of 80 MHz and 7 of 160 MHz.
Two channels interfere in proportion to the spectrum they share: a co-channel network occupies the whole block, while a 2.4 GHz network five channels away shares none of it.
